etymology: From the Hebrew 'Eben ha-'ezer, “stone of help,” compounding 'eben (stone) and 'ezer (help, aid).
biblical_def: Ebenezer is the memorial stone Samuel set up between Mizpeh and Shen after the LORD thundered against the Philistines and routed them, the prophet declaring, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1 Sam 7:12). The name is itself a sermon in granite: it does not commemorate Israel's valor but the bare, undeserved help of God, given to a people who had only just put away their strange gods and turned again unto the LORD. The stone fixes the eye not on the victory but on the Victor, teaching that every deliverance is mercy and not wages. Reformed piety has long seized upon Ebenezer as the type of the believer's grateful remembrance, for the same God who helped at Mizpeh is the rock of our salvation, and the true Stone of Help is Christ, the tried and precious cornerstone on whom the church is built and against whom the gates of hell shall not prevail. As Israel raised a stone to mark grace already received, so the saint looks back over a life of preservation and confesses that he has been carried thus far by no strength of his own. The monument therefore preaches assurance: He who has helped hitherto will not abandon His work, but will perfect that which concerneth us unto the day of Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: A memorial stone whose name means “stone of help,” raised by Samuel to commemorate God's deliverance of Israel.
webster_full: EBENEZER, noun (place). From the Hebrew 'eben, stone, and 'ezer, help; the stone of help.
A monument or memorial stone, raised in token of divine assistance received.
The proper name of the spot where Samuel set up the stone, between Mizpeh and Shen.

As the LORD had helped Israel against the Philistines, so the stone was named for an enduring witness: “Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.” (1 Sam 7:12)
Figuratively, any standing token of thankful remembrance for past mercies.
scriptures: Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out against the Philistines to battle, and pitched beside Ebenezer: and the Philistines pitched in Aphek.
My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
corruption_summary: The word is more often sentimentalized into a vague nostalgia than openly redefined.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Where Ebenezer is misused it is chiefly through sentiment—treated as a warm token of personal milestones rather than a confession that the help came wholly from the LORD. The principle to recover is that a true Ebenezer points away from the worshipper and toward the God of free grace; it is a stone of His help, not a trophy of our progress.

The recovery, then, is doxological remembrance. Reformed faith raises its memorials not to flatter the saint but to silence his boasting, for the same sovereign mercy that delivered Israel at Mizpeh sustains the believer hourly. To say “hitherto hath the LORD helped us” is to ground assurance in the unchanging Helper, and so to face the future without fear.
roots_summary: Ebenezer joins the common Hebrew nouns for stone and help into a single memorial confession.
roots_lines: 'eben — stone, the same word used of the foundation stone laid in Zion.
'ezer — help, succour; used of God as Israel's helper and shield.
The construct 'Eben ha-'ezer binds the two: “the stone of the help.”
The cognate verb 'azar means to gird, aid, or come to the rescue.
The same root 'ezer names the woman in Genesis 2:18, a help answering to man.
usage: Of the literal monument Samuel erected after the rout of the Philistines.
Of the place-name marking the field of earlier defeat and later deliverance.
Figuratively in Christian devotion, of any grateful marker of God's past faithfulness.

etymology: From the Hebrew Beyth-'El, “house of God,” from bayith (house) and 'El (God).
biblical_def: Bethel means “house of God,” the name Jacob gave to the place where, fleeing Esau, he saw in a dream a ladder set up on the earth whose top reached to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the LORD standing above it renewing the covenant promise (Gen 28:10-22). Awaking, Jacob confessed, “Surely the LORD is in this place,” anointed the stone of his pillow, and vowed. Our Lord Himself unveils the ladder's meaning, declaring that He is the way between heaven and earth, the true Bethel where God and man meet (John 1:51). Bethel thus stands as a type of Christ, the one mediator and the living house of God. Yet the place became a parable of how true worship is debased into idolatry, for Jeroboam, fearing the pull of Jerusalem, set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan, ordained unauthorized priests, and devised a feast out of his own heart (1 Kgs 12:28-33). The house of God was made a house of calves. Bethel therefore teaches a double lesson: where God meets His people there is grace and a ladder to heaven, but where men invent their own worship the holiest name becomes a shrine of sin. The remedy is to worship only as God has commanded, through the Mediator He has appointed.
webster_summary: “House of God”; the place of Jacob's ladder and vow, later seat of Jeroboam's calf-worship.
webster_full: BETHEL, noun (place). From the Hebrew bayith, house, and 'El, God; the house of God.
A place in the hill country of Ephraim, originally called Luz, renamed by Jacob.
The site of Jacob's vision of a ladder reaching to heaven and of his solemn vow.
Later one of the two royal shrines where Jeroboam set a golden calf: “And he set the one in Bethel, and the other put he in Dan.” (1 Kgs 12:29)
Figuratively, a place where God is present and worshipped—or, when corrupted, a monument to false worship.
scriptures: And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
And he called the name of that place Bethel: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Amo 5:5
But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought.
corruption_summary: The chief danger is the ancient one Bethel itself displays—will-worship dressed in the name of God—rather than a modern academic redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bethel's warning is timeless: Jeroboam did not deny God but reinvented His worship for convenience, and the same impulse animates every age that prefers worship devised “out of his own heart” to worship commanded in Scripture. The principle to recover is the regulative pattern—that God is to be worshipped in the way He has appointed, not in ways men find expedient or pleasing.

The recovery is reverent obedience. The same place that was once the gate of heaven became a snare because men kept the holy name while abandoning the holy command. Bethel thus presses upon the church the abiding rule that nearness to God is found only through His appointed Mediator and His appointed means, never through golden substitutes of our own making.
roots_summary: Bethel is a transparent Hebrew compound naming a dwelling of deity.
roots_lines: bayith — house, dwelling, household; the common Hebrew word for home.
'El — God, the strong One; the ancient Semitic name for deity.
Together Beyth-'El — “house of God,” the very gate of heaven.
The earlier name of the city was Luz, meaning almond or hazel.
The contrasting shrine-name Beth-aven, “house of vanity,” was later flung at corrupted Bethel by the prophets.
usage: Of the literal city and sanctuary in the hill country of Ephraim.
Of the place of Jacob's ladder, taken as a type of Christ the mediator.
Of the corrupted shrine of Jeroboam's calf-worship, a byword for false religion.

etymology: From the Greek Pergamos (also Pergamum), a city of Mysia in Asia Minor; the name is connected with a word for citadel or fortified height.
biblical_def: Pergamos was the third of the seven churches of Asia addressed by the risen Christ in the Revelation, the assembly dwelling “even where Satan's seat is” (Rev 2:13). The city was a stronghold of pagan religion—altar of Zeus, temple of the emperor-cult, shrine of the serpent-god of healing—so that the church lived under the very throne of organized idolatry. Christ commends them: they held fast His name and did not deny the faith even in the days of Antipas, His faithful martyr who was slain among them. Yet He rebukes them sharply, for some held the doctrine of Balaam and of the Nicolaitanes, tolerating compromise with idol-feasts and fornication. The peril of Pergamos is therefore not open persecution but creeping accommodation, the temptation to make peace with the surrounding darkness rather than to overcome it. The Lord calls them to repent, threatening to fight against the compromisers with the sword of His mouth, and promising to the overcomer hidden manna and a white stone with a new name. Pergamos stands as the type of every faithful remnant set down in hostile territory: called to confess Christ unflinchingly, to refuse the syncretism that would dilute the gospel, and to look beyond the seat of Satan to the throne of the Lamb who feeds His own with bread the world cannot see.
webster_summary: A city of Asia Minor, seat of pagan worship, and home of one of the seven churches commended for faithfulness yet rebuked for compromise.
webster_full: PERGAMOS, noun (place). From the Greek Pergamos, a fortified city of Mysia in Asia Minor.
A center of emperor-worship and pagan temples in the apostolic age.
The seat of one of the seven churches of Asia addressed in the Revelation.
The dwelling of a faithful confessing remnant amid idolatry: “I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is.” (Rev 2:13)
Figuratively, any church called to stand firm where the powers of darkness are entrenched.
scriptures: Rev 2:12
And to the angel of the church in Pergamos write; These things saith he which hath the sharp sword with two edges;
Rev 2:13

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
Rev 2:16
Repent; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.
Rev 2:17

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
corruption_summary: Pergamos' lesson—compromise with the surrounding culture—is itself the corruption it warns against, perennially urged upon the church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The doctrine of Balaam and of the Nicolaitanes was a counsel of accommodation: blend with the idol-feasts, soften the edges of the faith, keep the peace with a hostile world. That same counsel is pressed on the church today under gentler names, and the principle to recover is the unbending confession of Christ's name even where Satan's seat is.

The recovery is holy nonconformity. Antipas held fast and was slain; the overcomer is promised hidden manna no compromiser tastes. Pergamos thus teaches that the gospel is not preserved by negotiation with the age but by faithful endurance, and that the sword of Christ's mouth falls upon a tolerant church as surely as upon the world it courted.
roots_summary: The name derives from the Greek city and its sense of a fortified citadel.
roots_lines: Pergamos / Pergamon — the Greek name of the Mysian capital, linked to a word for height or citadel.
The English “parchment” descends from pergamēnē, the writing-skin named for this city.
thronos tou Satana — “Satan's seat,” the throne-like altar dominating the acropolis.
Antipas — “against all,” the named martyr who stood when others bent.
Nikolaitēs — the sect whose name suggests “conquering the people,” teaching license.
usage: Of the literal city of Pergamos in Roman Asia.
Of the apostolic church addressed by Christ in the second chapter of Revelation.
Figuratively, of any faithful congregation surrounded by entrenched ungodliness.

etymology: English “rod” for the Hebrew matteh, a staff or branch; named for Aaron, the first high priest, whose name is of uncertain Hebrew or Egyptian origin.
biblical_def: Aaron's rod is the almond staff that budded, blossomed, and bore ripe almonds overnight in the tabernacle, the LORD's own miraculous verdict in the rebellion of Korah confirming that Aaron and his house alone were chosen to the priesthood (Num 17). When the twelve tribal rods were laid up before the testimony, Aaron's alone broke into life, and the LORD commanded it kept before the ark for a token against the rebels, that murmuring against His ordained priest might cease. The writer to the Hebrews tells us it was laid up within the ark itself, beside the golden pot of manna and the tables of the covenant (Heb 9:4). A dead stick brought to fruitfulness is a vivid type of resurrection: out of barren wood God draws blossom and fruit, as out of death He raises life. More directly it points to Christ, our great High Priest, whose priesthood is not self-assumed but divinely confirmed—confirmed supremely by His rising from the dead, for it was not possible that He should be holden of death. As Aaron's budding rod silenced the rebels and sealed his office, so the empty tomb seals the everlasting priesthood of the Son, who ever liveth to make intercession. The faithful, contemplating this fruitful rod, learn to rest in a priest God Himself has owned.
webster_summary: The almond staff that miraculously budded to confirm Aaron's priesthood, later kept within the ark.
webster_full: AARON'S ROD, noun (sacred object). From the Hebrew matteh, a staff or branch, and the name of Aaron, Israel's first high priest.
The staff laid up before the testimony that budded, bloomed, and yielded almonds in a single night.
A divinely wrought sign confirming the priesthood of Aaron's house against the murmuring of Israel.

An object kept within the ark of the covenant: “And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded.” (Num 17:8)
Figuratively, a token of life raised out of deadness, and of an office sealed by God Himself.
scriptures: Num 17:8

And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Bring Aaron's rod again before the testimony, to be kept for a token against the rebels; and thou shalt quite take away their murmurings from me, that they die not.
Heb 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
Heb 5:4
And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.
corruption_summary: The object is largely neglected rather than redefined; its typological force is the casualty of inattention.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Aaron's rod is more often skipped as an obscure relic than openly twisted, and the loss is the surrender of its rich typology. The principle to recover is that this budding staff is a deliberate sign—life from a dead branch, a priesthood confirmed by God and not by men—pointing forward to the resurrection and the everlasting priesthood of Christ.

The recovery is typological reading under the rule of Scripture. Hebrews itself draws the line from the rod within the ark to the High Priest within the veil, so the church need not invent meanings but receive the ones the Spirit has given. To behold the rod that budded is to be steadied in the One whose office death could not silence.
roots_summary: The phrase joins the Hebrew word for staff with the name of the first high priest.
roots_lines: matteh — rod, staff, branch; also used of a tribe, since each tribe carried a rod.
'Aharon — Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's first high priest.
The rod was of shaqed, almond, the “watching” tree, first to bloom in spring.
Related shaqad means to watch or hasten, fitting the almond's early budding.
The fruit-bearing of a cut staff serves as a Hebrew emblem of resurrection life.
usage: Of the literal staff that budded to vindicate Aaron's priesthood.
Of the relic laid up within the ark of the covenant.
Figuratively, of life raised from deadness and a priesthood confirmed by God.

etymology: From the Latin census, a registering or numbering of the people, from censēre, to assess or rate.
biblical_def: A census in Scripture is the numbering of Israel, and it is hedged about with holy fear. When the LORD commanded the count in the wilderness (Num 1), He bound it to a ransom: at every numbering each man twenty years old and upward was to give a half shekel, “a ransom for his soul,” that there be no plague among them when they were numbered (Exo 30:11-16). The reason is solemn—to number Israel is to lay hold of what belongs to God, and unless atonement is acknowledged the act becomes presumption. This is why David's census, undertaken in pride and without that ransom owned, brought a devastating plague upon the land (2 Sam 24). The same act, performed in obedient dependence, is blessing; performed in self-glorying autonomy, it is sin that costs the lives of thousands. The theology is unmistakable: man does not own his fellow man, and even to count souls one must confess they are ransomed and not one's own. The half-shekel pointed beyond itself to redemption by price, fulfilled when the Son of man gave His life a ransom for many. Every soul stands before God as one purchased, the rich man's no dearer and the poor man's no cheaper, for the price was the same precious blood. The census thus teaches that life is God's, numbered souls are ransomed souls, and pride in our own strength invites the plague.
webster_summary: The official numbering of the people, commanded with a ransom in the law and judged when undertaken in pride.
webster_full: CENSUS, noun (Mosaic ordinance). From the Latin census, a registering and rating of the people.
An enumeration of the inhabitants of a nation, especially the men fit for war.
In Israel, a numbering bound by law to the payment of a half-shekel ransom.

An act of presumption when done in self-glory: “And David's heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the LORD, I have sinned greatly in that I have done.” (2 Sam 24:10)
Figuratively, any reckoning or accounting of persons or things.
scriptures: Num 1:2
Take ye the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, after their families, by the house of their fathers, with the number of their names, every male by their polls;

When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them.
And again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.

And David's heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the LORD, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O LORD, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.
corruption_summary: The census is more often misread as an arbitrary punishment than redefined by modern ideology.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The common stumbling is the charge that God arbitrarily punished a mere head-count; the principle to recover is that the law itself attached a ransom to every numbering, so David's sin lay in counting souls as his own asset in pride rather than confessing them as ransomed and belonging to the LORD.

The recovery is reverence for the ownership of God over human life. The half-shekel taught Israel that no man may be tallied as property, for each is bought, and the price is the same for rich and poor. Read so, the census magnifies redemption by price and points to the Son of man who gave His life a ransom for many.
roots_summary: The English word renders a Latin term for numbering, behind which stands the Hebrew act of taking the sum of the people.
roots_lines: census (Latin) — a registering and rating of citizens.
censēre — to assess, estimate, or judge worth.
Hebrew paqad — to number, muster, visit, or appoint.
Hebrew nasa' rosh — literally “to lift the head,” the idiom for taking a census.
Hebrew kopher — ransom, covering price, the half-shekel each numbered man paid.
usage: Of the lawful numbering of Israel commanded by God with its required ransom.
Of David's sinful census and the plague it provoked.
Of the half-shekel atonement money laid up for the service of the tabernacle.

etymology: English “unclean” rendering the Hebrew tame', ceremonially defiled or impure, set over against tahor, clean.
biblical_def: The unclean animals are the creatures the law of Moses forbade Israel to eat or touch, distinguished in Leviticus 11 from the clean by signs such as the parted hoof and the chewing of the cud, fins and scales in the waters, and a list of forbidden birds and creeping things. The purpose was not hygienic theory but holiness: “Ye shall be holy; for I am holy,” the dietary lines marking Israel off from the nations as a separated, set-apart people. Every meal became a catechism in distinction, training the conscience to discern between the holy and the profane, the clean and the unclean. These distinctions were ceremonial, not moral, and so they belonged to the schoolmaster era that pointed forward to Christ. In the gospel that era closes: our Lord, declaring His word, “purging all meats” (Mark 7:19), pronounced the heart, not the stomach, the seat of defilement. To Peter the great sheet descended thrice with all manner of beasts and the command, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:9-16)—a vision whose deeper meaning was the cleansing of the Gentiles and their gathering into the one new man. Thus the abrogation of the food-laws is no loosening of holiness but its fulfilment: the wall of separation falls because the substance has come, and the people of God, no longer divided by table, are made one in Christ, called still to be holy, now by faith and the Spirit rather than by meats and drinks.
webster_summary: Creatures forbidden to Israel by the ceremonial law as ritually impure, whose distinctions were fulfilled and set aside in Christ.
webster_full: UNCLEAN ANIMALS, noun (Mosaic law). From the Hebrew tame', ceremonially defiled, opposed to tahor, clean.
Beasts, fish, fowl, and creeping things which the law of Moses forbade Israel to eat or touch.
Marked out by ritual signs that taught separation between the holy and the profane.
Declared clean under the gospel: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” (Acts 10:15)
Figuratively, of moral and spiritual impurity from which the believer is to keep himself.
scriptures: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
Mar 7:19
Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats?
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
corruption_summary: The food-laws are misread either as primitive hygiene or as still binding, against their plain ceremonial purpose and clear abrogation in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors are older: to flatten the laws into ancient dietary science, or to insist they still bind the Christian conscience. The principle to recover is the Reformed distinction of the law—these were ceremonial ordinances marking Israel's separation, abrogated when their substance, Christ, came; the moral law's call to holiness abides, but its ritual shadow does not.

The recovery is to read the food-laws as fulfilled, not merely cancelled. Our Lord purged all meats and Peter's sheet declared the Gentiles clean; the wall between Jew and Gentile fell because the one new man was formed. To honor these texts is to confess both the law's wise design and the gospel's glorious liberty—still holy, no longer divided by the table.
roots_summary: The category rests on the Hebrew opposition of the clean and the unclean within the ceremonial law.
roots_lines: tame' — unclean, defiled, ritually impure.
tahor — clean, pure, fit for use or worship.
sheqets — an abomination or detestable thing, used of forbidden creatures.
qadosh — holy, set apart; the goal the distinctions served.
Greek koinos — common or unclean, the word in Peter's vision now overturned.
usage: Of the literal beasts, birds, and creeping things forbidden to Israel by the law.
Of the ceremonial distinction between clean and unclean, abrogated in Christ.
Figuratively, of moral impurity from which the saint is to keep separate.

etymology: English “atonement” (at-one-ment, reconciliation) rendering the Hebrew kippurim, with kesef ha-kippurim, the money of the atonements; the ransom-price paid at a numbering.
biblical_def: The atonement money is the half shekel each Israelite man was to give “a ransom for his soul unto the LORD” whenever the people were numbered, that no plague break out among them (Exo 30:11-16). It was levied without distinction of estate: “The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel.” The flat, identical price preaches a profound doctrine—before God every soul is of equal account, and every soul stands in equal need of ransom. No man could buy a fuller redemption with greater wealth, nor was the poor man's soul redeemed for a smaller sum, for the value lay not in the coin but in the atonement it confessed. The silver was appointed for the service of the tabernacle, a perpetual memorial before the LORD that the people were a ransomed people. As a type it points unerringly to Christ, who is Himself the ransom for many, not silver and gold but His own precious blood, by which He purchased a redeemed people out of every kindred. The half-shekel could only signify; the cross accomplishes. And as the price was one and the same for all, so the redemption in Christ levels every distinction: there is neither rich nor poor, bond nor free, at the foot of the cross, for all are bought at the one infinite price. The atonement money therefore teaches the equality of souls before God and the singular, sufficient ransom found only in the blood of the Lamb.
webster_summary: The half-shekel ransom paid by every Israelite at a numbering, a type of redemption by a single price.
webster_full: ATONEMENT MONEY, noun (Mosaic ordinance). From the Hebrew kesef ha-kippurim, the money of the atonements; a ransom for the soul.
The half shekel required of every numbered Israelite as a ransom for his life.
A sum laid up and appointed for the service of the tabernacle.

A price equal for every man, high or low: “The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls.” (Exo 30:15)
Figuratively, a token of the one ransom-price by which souls are redeemed.
scriptures: This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD.
The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls.

And thou shalt take the atonement money of the children of Israel, and shalt appoint it for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation; that it may be a memorial unto the children of Israel before the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls.
Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
corruption_summary: The ordinance is more neglected than redefined; its teaching on the equal price of every soul is the casualty of inattention.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The atonement money is rarely attacked, only overlooked; the principle to recover is its plain doctrine—the rich gave no more and the poor no less, so that every soul is reckoned of equal account before God and stands in equal need of ransom.

The recovery is to see the half-shekel as a finger pointing to the cross. It could confess redemption but never accomplish it; only the precious blood of Christ, the one price for all the redeemed, levels every distinction and purchases a people for God. To honor the ordinance is to magnify the singular, sufficient ransom of the Lamb.
roots_summary: The phrase joins the doctrine of atonement to the ransom-price required at every numbering.
roots_lines: kopher — ransom, a covering price paid to redeem a forfeited life.
kippurim — atonements, coverings; the root behind the Day of Atonement.
kesef — silver, money; the substance of the half-shekel.
beqa' — the half-shekel weight, “a bekah for every man.”
shekel ha-qodesh — the shekel of the sanctuary, the appointed standard of weight.
usage: Of the literal half-shekel ransom paid at a numbering of Israel.
Of the silver appointed for the service and memorial of the tabernacle.
Figuratively, of the one ransom-price by which Christ redeems His people.

etymology: English “covenant” for the Hebrew berith, a binding agreement, joined with melach, salt; berith melach, a covenant of salt.
biblical_def: A covenant of salt is a covenant declared perpetual and incorruptible, the LORD attaching salt—the preserving, unchanging element—as the seal of an enduring bond. He gives the priestly portions to Aaron and his sons “by a statute for ever… it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19); He establishes the kingdom over Israel to David and his sons “by a covenant of salt” (2 Chr 13:5); and He commands that with every meal offering salt be offered, “the salt of the covenant of thy God” (Lev 2:13). Salt preserves from corruption, seasons, and does not decay; in the ancient world to eat salt with another was to enter a bond of loyalty. The figure therefore declares that God's covenant does not rot or fail with time but endures, faithful and unbreakable, because it rests on His own unchanging character. This points to the everlasting covenant of grace, ordered in all things and sure, which God keeps not for an hour but for ever, and which is fulfilled and made perpetual in Christ, the Mediator of a better covenant established upon better promises. The salt that seasoned the offerings also instructs the saints, whom our Lord calls the salt of the earth, to be incorruptible and faithful, having salt in themselves and peace one with another. The covenant of salt thus assures the believer that the bond God has made with His people in His Son shall never lose its savour nor be dissolved.
webster_summary: A covenant marked as perpetual and incorruptible, salt signifying its enduring, unbreakable nature.
webster_full: COVENANT OF SALT, noun (Mosaic covenant-sign). From the Hebrew berith, covenant, and melach, salt; an everlasting and incorruptible bond.
A solemn agreement confirmed as perpetual, salt being the emblem of permanence.
The priestly portions and the kingdom of David, both granted by such a covenant.
An ordinance requiring salt with every offering: “with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.” (Lev 2:13)
Figuratively, any bond of unfailing fidelity and incorruptible faithfulness.
scriptures: All the heave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer unto the LORD, have I given thee, and thy sons and thy daughters with thee, by a statute for ever: it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD unto thee and to thy seed with thee.
Lev 2:13

And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.
Ought ye not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?
Mar 9:50
Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another.
corruption_summary: The phrase is largely forgotten rather than redefined; its witness to the permanence of God's covenant is what suffers neglect.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The covenant of salt is seldom attacked, only overlooked; the principle to recover is its plain assurance—salt preserves and does not decay, and so God's covenant with His people endures unbroken, resting upon His own unchanging faithfulness.

The recovery is to read salt as the pledge of an everlasting covenant fulfilled in Christ. He is the Mediator of a better covenant, ordered in all things and sure, which cannot lose its savour. The same salt seasons the saints, calling them to incorruptible loyalty and peace, having salt in themselves as the people of an unfailing God.
roots_summary: The expression binds the Hebrew word for covenant to the preserving element of salt.
roots_lines: berith — covenant, a binding and solemn agreement.
melach — salt; emblem of preservation and incorruption.
berith melach — “covenant of salt,” a perpetual, unbreakable bond.
'olam — for ever, everlasting; the duration the salt-covenant signifies.
Greek halas — salt, the word our Lord uses of His disciples as the salt of the earth.
usage: Of the perpetual grant of the priestly portions to Aaron's house.
Of the everlasting kingdom granted to David by a covenant of salt.
Figuratively, of any incorruptible bond of fidelity, and of the saints as salt.

etymology: English “commandment” for the Hebrew mitsvah, a precept or charge; the fifth word of the Decalogue, “Honour thy father and thy mother.”
biblical_def: The fifth commandment is the first word of the second table of the law: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Exo 20:12). Standing at the head of our duties to men, it is the root of all lawful authority and obedience. The honour owed to father and mother is, in the Reformed reading of the law, the pattern and fountain of every relation of superior and inferior—in the family, the church, the commonwealth, and the workplace—so that this one precept teaches reverence, submission, and dutiful love wherever God has set authority over us. The apostle calls it “the first commandment with promise” (Eph 6:1-3), for to its keeping is annexed the pledge of length of days and well-being, a promise the New Testament applies to the children of the church. This complementarian order is not an arrangement of human convenience but a created and commanded structure: God ordains fathers and mothers, magistrates and pastors, masters and elders, and binds the conscience to honour them in the Lord. The commandment is fulfilled and adorned in Christ, the perfect Son, who was subject to His earthly parents, obedient to His heavenly Father unto death, and now reigns as the Head over all. He keeps the law His people break and supplies in His obedience the honour we have withheld. Thus the fifth commandment both governs the home and points to the gospel, where the obedient Son secures the inheritance for adopted children.
webster_summary: The Decalogue's charge to honour father and mother, the first commandment with promise and the root of lawful authority.
webster_full: FIFTH COMMANDMENT, noun (moral law). From the Hebrew mitsvah, a precept; the fifth word of the Decalogue.
The precept requiring honour and obedience to father and mother.
The head of the second table, governing all relations of authority and submission.
The first commandment with promise: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.” (Exo 20:12)
Figuratively, the foundation of order in family, church, and commonwealth.
scriptures: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
Eph 6:2
Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;)
Eph 6:1
Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
Col 3:20
Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord.
corruption_summary: The commandment is pressed hard by an age that resents all settled authority and the ordered structure of the family.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the spirit of the age corrodes it by exalting personal autonomy above every duty owed to parents and lawful superiors, treating honour as optional and authority as suspect. The principle to recover is that God Himself ordains the offices of father and mother, and that to honour them in the Lord is the root of all rightful order in family, church, and state.

The recovery is glad submission within God's created structure. The commandment carries a promise, binding obedience to blessing, and it is no burden but a fountain of well-being. It is fulfilled in Christ the perfect Son, obedient to His parents and to His Father unto death, whose righteousness covers the dishonour His people have shown and secures the inheritance for the adopted children of God.
roots_summary: The commandment rests on the Hebrew words for honour and for father and mother within the Decalogue.
roots_lines: kabed — to honour; literally to count weighty, to give due reverence.
'ab — father; head of the household and of authority.
'em — mother; honoured equally with the father in the precept.
mitsvah — commandment, precept, charge from God.
Greek timaō — to honour, the verb Paul uses in citing the commandment.
usage: Of the literal charge to honour one's father and mother.
Of the broader duty of reverence to all lawful authority God has set over us.
Of the commandment's promise of length of days and well-being to the obedient.

etymology: English “ordinance” from the Latin ordinare, to set in order; the appointments God instituted at creation, before the fall.
biblical_def: The creation ordinances are the standing institutions God appointed at the beginning, before sin entered, and which therefore bind all mankind in every age. Three are commonly numbered: marriage, labour with dominion, and the Sabbath. God made man male and female and joined them in marriage, declaring, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24); He gave the dominion-mandate, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it,” and set the man in the garden “to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 1:28; 2:15); and He hallowed the seventh day, resting from His work and sanctifying it (Gen 2:2-3). These ordinances are not Mosaic and ceremonial but creational and perpetual, woven into the order of the world by the Maker's own hand. They are not abolished by the fall but preserved through it, though now pursued amid thorns and toil. Our Lord confirms marriage as a creation ordinance, appealing past the law of Moses to “the beginning” (Matt 19), and the New Testament establishes the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath, the weekly rest fulfilled and renewed in Christ's resurrection. Christ Himself is the last Adam, who keeps the dominion-mandate by subduing all His enemies, who takes the church as His bride in a marriage of which Eden's was the type, and who gives His people the true rest that the Sabbath foreshadowed. The creation ordinances thus order human life under God and find their consummation in the work of the second Adam.
webster_summary: The pre-fall institutions of marriage, labour and dominion, and the Sabbath, ordained at creation and binding on all mankind.
webster_full: CREATION ORDINANCES, noun (creational law). From the Latin ordinare, to set in order; the appointments God instituted at the beginning.
Standing institutions established before the fall and binding upon all men.
Commonly numbered as marriage, labour with dominion, and the Sabbath rest.
Grounded in the work of the first week: “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.” (Gen 2:3)
Figuratively, the created framework within which human life is rightly ordered.
scriptures: Gen 1:28

And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
Gen 2:3
And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.
Gen 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
corruption_summary: The creation ordinances are openly assailed by an age that severs marriage, labour, and rest from their created design.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet each ordinance is pressed by the spirit of the age—marriage redefined against its created form of one man and one woman, labour resented or worshipped, and rest swallowed by ceaseless toil or idleness. The principle to recover is that these are creational and perpetual, ordained before the fall and binding on all mankind, not arrangements men may renegotiate.

The recovery is to honour the Maker's order from the beginning, as our Lord did when He appealed past Moses to creation itself. Marriage, dominion, and Sabbath are preserved through the fall and find their consummation in Christ the last Adam, who weds His church, subdues every foe, and gives the true rest the seventh day foreshadowed.
roots_summary: The phrase joins the doctrine of creation to the Latin sense of an appointed order.
roots_lines: ordinare (Latin) — to set in order, arrange, appoint.
Hebrew bara' — to create; the act establishing these standing appointments.
Hebrew shabath — to cease or rest; the root of Sabbath.
Hebrew radah — to have dominion, rule; the dominion-mandate.
Hebrew dabaq — to cleave or cling; the bond of one-flesh marriage.
usage: Of the three pre-fall institutions of marriage, labour, and the Sabbath.
Of the perpetual, creational law binding all mankind apart from Moses.
Of the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath fulfilled in Christ's resurrection.
